title: Erasmus on the flood of printed books
body: Erasmus, a Latin scholar and a Catholic reformer, criticised the excesses of Catholicism but kept his distance from Martin Luther. In his Adages (1508) he expressed deep anxiety about printing. He asked to what corner of the world these swarms of new books did not fly. He granted that one book here and there might contribute something worth knowing, but argued that their very multitude was hurtful to scholarship because it created a glut, and that even in good things excess was harmful. Printers, he complained, filled the world not only with trifling books but with stupid, ignorant, slanderous, scandalous, raving, irreligious and seditious ones, so many that even valuable publications lost their value.

title: Books, libraries and working people
body: In nineteenth-century Madras towns, very cheap small books were brought to markets and sold at crossroads, so that poor people travelling to markets could buy them. Public libraries were set up from the early twentieth century, but they were located mostly in cities and towns, and at times in prosperous villages; for rich local patrons, setting up a library was a way of acquiring prestige. Factory workers were usually too overworked and lacked the education to write much about their lives, though a few, like Kashibaba of Kanpur, did publish. By the 1930s, Bangalore cotton millworkers set up libraries to educate themselves, following the example of Bombay workers. These libraries were sponsored by social reformers who tried to restrict excessive drinking, to bring literacy and, sometimes, to spread the message of nationalism.

title: Press, repression and protest
body: Despite repressive measures, nationalist newspapers grew in number in all parts of India, reporting colonial misrule and encouraging nationalist activities. When Punjab revolutionaries were deported in 1907, Balgangadhar Tilak wrote with great sympathy about them in his Kesari; this led to his imprisonment in 1908, which in turn provoked widespread protests all over India. During the First World War, under the Defence of India Rules, 22 newspapers had to furnish securities, and 18 of them shut down rather than comply. At the outbreak of the Second World War, the Defence of India Act allowed censoring of war-related reports, and in August 1942 about 90 newspapers were suppressed. In 1922 Gandhi said that the fight for Swaraj meant, before all else, a fight for liberty of speech, liberty of the press and freedom of association.
